title: Accelerator swap + capacity add: on-call runbook and incident notes (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This draft is intended for on-call SREs and platform engineers who need a concise, low-friction playbook for:
- hot/hot-swap replacement of failed accelerators (NVIDIA/AMD TPU-like cards),
- safe cordon/drain of nodes serving latency-sensitive inference,
- cluster recovery patterns after multi-node loss, and
- ordered capacity additions (one-off GPUs or pool expansion) with traffic stabilization.

Tone: operational checklist + short context + commands. Not exhaustive — use with pager/resolution channel open.

Quick context notes (recent learnings):
- Inference pods are sensitive to cold-KV-cache misses. When draining nodes with heavy prefix cache hits, expect 60–200ms tail latency spikes if cache isn't warm on destination nodes.
- Autoscaler (cluster-autoscaler variant) can interact poorly with aggressive cordon/drain schedules; prefer manual stepwise capacity increase in high-load windows.
- PCIe reset vs full host reboot: some accelerator faults are resolved by driver rebind and module reload; full node replacement should be last resort during business hours.

Pre-swap checklist (before touching hardware or triggering node maintenance):
- Check alerts and scope: identify affected pods, node labels (gpu-type, pool), and model versions. Command: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Running --selector=app=redwood-inference -n inference | grep <node-name>
- Confirm fallback capacity: ensure other GPU pool has >= 20% spare capacity or that Dedicated pool autoscaler target is above current load.
- Notify stakeholders: post to #prod-infra and #oncall (include incident id), set incident channel (Slack).
- Reserve time window: avoid replacements during global rollouts or heavy benchmark windows.
- Backup: snapshot important node-level debug info (dmesg, nvidia-smi -q, /var/log/messages).

Hardware quick-fixes (try before full replacement):
1) Soft reset driver: ssh to node, sudo systemctl stop inference-agent; sudo rmmod nvidia_uvm nvidia; sudo modprobe nvidia; sudo systemctl start inference-agent.
2) PCIe rebind: echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<device>/reset (verify device id).
3) Power-cycle the PCIe slot via BMC if available (IPMI commands), then verify with nvidia-smi.
If any hardware quick-fix successful, run validation script: /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-smoke-test.sh and mark node healthy in monitoring.

Node cordon & drain strategy (safest path for live clusters):
- Goal: move workload off the node with minimal service disruption and controlled cache-warmup.
- High-level approach: cordon -> staged drain (evict non-critical first) -> warmup destination pods -> finish drain -> uncordon (if maintenance aborted).

Commands and sequence (example):
1) Cordon the node to prevent new pods: kubectl cordon <node-name>
2) Annotate the node for maintenance window: kubectl annotate node <node-name> maintenance=accelerator-swap:$(date -Iminutes)
3) Identify critical inference pods (model traffic >= 5QPS or 95th-latency bound): kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CPU:.spec.containers[*].resources,k8sNode:.spec.nodeName -n inference | grep <node-name>
4) Drain non-critical pods first: kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='!redwood-critical' --grace-period=120 --timeout=20m
5) Warmup plan for critical pods: spawn temporary lightweight copies on target nodes with the same model weights but scaled to 10–20% traffic using traffic routing rules in the router (tag-based routing). Once KV cache warms (monitor prefetched KV hit rate), shift traffic gradually.
6) Finish drain of critical pods with lower-concurrency option: kubectl drain <node-name> --pod-selector='redwood-critical' --force --grace-period=300 --timeout=30m
7) If drain fails due to eviction PDBs, contact app owner to temporarily relax PDBs or perform coordinated rolling restart.

Special notes about KV/prefix caches and seq len:
- If models use long KV cache (context > 1k tokens), re-routing a single request can re-warm caches slowly; prefer phasing traffic in increments (10 -> 30 -> 60 -> 100%).
- Use built-in cache prefill endpoint /debug/cache/prefill on destination pods to pre-warm for a set of prompt prefixes.

Cluster recovery pattern (after partial outage or multi-node loss):
1) Assess cluster state: kubectl get nodes, kubectl get cs; check scheduler backlog and pod pending reasons.
2) Prioritize control-plane and scheduler health first. If API server is degraded, escalate to platform-engineering.
3) Triage pods in Pending: describe pod to find reason (Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu, failed attach, CrashLoopBackOff).
4) If insufficient GPU capacity, follow capacity-add steps below. If attach/driver failures, consider cordoning and rebooting affected nodes after driver reinstall.
5) Reinflate routing: move traffic away from degraded region/pool via the smart-router (policy: fallback-regions).

Capacity addition (ordered steps for adding GPUs or expanding a GPU pool):
Pre-add checks:
- Confirm image compatibility and driver revision tested on new GPU type.
- Capacity plan: expected QPS per GPU, estimated warmup time, and autoscaler settings.
- Lock rolling deploys for 30 min (avoid simultaneous model/pipeline changes).

Add flow (for cloud-backed pool):
1) Provision nodes via infra pipeline (Terraform/Cloud API). Tag nodes with pool=dedicated-accelerator-v2 and gpu-type labels.
2) Wait for node bootstrap and kubelet registration: kubectl get nodes --selector=pool=dedicated-accelerator-v2
3) Run smoke tests (gpu-smoke-test.sh) on new nodes.
4) Add to scheduler with taints only if needed, or mark schedulable.
5) Gradually shift routing weight to new nodes/pool: use router to send 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over 10–30 minute intervals, watching 99th latency, error rate, and token costs.
6) If latency or error rates spike > SLO thresholds, rollback weight immediately and investigate.

Post-add validations and hardening:
- Verify cost metrics and token-per-second throughput.
- Add new nodes to instance group autoscaler config and tests.
- Document driver/kernel versions in asset inventory.

Escalation matrix (who to call):
- Level 1: on-call SRE (first responder) — try driver reset + drain plan.
- Level 2: infra-ops (Diego Ramos) — hardware BMC/IPMI, scheduled maintenance window for physical replacement.
- Level 3: runtime team (Maya Chen) — model-serving config, KV cache strategies, router weight changes.
- Level 4: platform leads / exec on-call — if outage > 2 hours or revenue-impacting.

Incident review template (to fill after event):
- Incident ID:
- Timeline: short bullet minutes-since-detect -> action -> result
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence (logs, kernel oops, driver stack traces)
- What worked well (e.g., temporary routing to fallback pool)
- What didn't (e.g., autoscaler thrash, manual BMC steps required)
- Action items (owner + due date):
  * e.g., "Add cache prefill endpoint to smoke tests" — Maya — 2026-03-15
  * "Document vendor PCIe reset procedure for rack X" — Diego — 2026-03-01
- Severity, customer impact and mitigations used

Operational tips and gotchas (collected from recent incidents):
- Avoid kubectl drain --force in the middle of high-volume TTL queues — it can cause cascading timeouts.
- Always verify the scheduler has alternate space (kubectl describe node <node> to see allocatable).
- For multi-tenant racks, a single accelerator failure may not trigger alerts if node remains up; watch per-GPU health (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv).
- Keep a small 'buffer' pool during major cloud provider maintenance windows.

Small smoke-test snippets (examples to run from oncall box):
- List GPU nodes: kubectl get nodes -l alpha.kubernetes.io/nvidia-gpu=true -o wide
- Check GPU usage on node (ssh): nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv -l 1
- Prefill cache (HTTP): curl -X POST https://<pod-ip>:8080/debug/cache/prefill -d '{"prompts": ["<common-prefix>"]}'
- Check pending pods reasons: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, reason: .status.conditions}'

Follow-ups to convert this draft into a final runbook:
- Add exact vendor/part numbers and power-cycling playbook (Diego).
- Bake prefill/warmup into autoscaler lifecycle hooks (Elliot).
- Add checklist for coordinated PDB relaxations with product owners and sample Slack templates for notifications.
- Run tabletop simulation next on-call rotation and capture metrics.

Appendix: quick links and references:
- Pager channel: #oncall (prod)
- Incident board: Linear INF-371 (see linked artifacts)
- Runtime PR: Replace GPU kernel selection logic (linked above)

Notes-to-self / TODOs (raw):
- insert standard times-to-warm values per model family (gpt3-like vs instruction tuned)
- capture latency deltas after drain in last weekend test
- template for Slack message that includes required fields: incident id, ETA to resolution, affected pools

End of draft.

Last edited by Asha Patel.
